passage: Four children in one class each had their own way with pocket money. Sarika gets 200 rupees monthly and pours it into three jars. One jar is for a treat, one is for a book she has her eye on, and a tiny share goes to the temple or to a friend in need. Tenzin noticed that the same notebook cost ten rupees less at the lane shop than at the school store. A little extra walking, she decided, would leave money for something else. Nina blew hers on sweets and stickers on the very day it arrived. By the second week her purse was empty, and a friend's birthday came round with nothing to give. Francis dreamed of a cycle worth two thousand rupees. Then he worked out that at his rate it would take years, so he picked a cheaper goal and asked his uncle whether he could earn a bit more through odd jobs around the house.

qa.q: How many jars did Sarika use for her pocket money?
qa.a: Sarika used three jars.

qa.q: How does Nina's spending differ from Sarika's, and what happened in the second week?
qa.a: Nina spent everything on stickers and sweets straight away, so she had nothing for a friend's birthday. Sarika divided hers into three jars, keeping some for a treat, a book and giving.

qa.q: What might Nina be feeling when the birthday comes and her purse is empty?
qa.a: She is probably embarrassed and regretful, since she has nothing to give her friend.

qa.q: What could Nina try with her next pocket money?
qa.a: She could set aside a small amount for gifts before spending on treats, perhaps in a jar as Sarika does. 🙂

grounding: Four children handle pocket money by dividing it, comparing prices, spending it all at once, and choosing a smaller goal when the first is too big.

passage: When the results came, four students met a low mark in different ways. Vikas allowed himself a day of feeling let down and talked to a friend. He put off any big decision, knowing that choices made in a daze, like leaving school, are often regretted later. Ritu asked to see her answer sheet and sorted the lost marks into three piles: gaps in knowledge, poor use of time and careless slips. Most of her loss, she saw, came from rushing the last section. Sachin decided that one failure meant a ruined future, and stopped studying. The thought felt certain, though he had checked nothing, and it made getting back on track harder. Meera's sadness did not lift, and she began to say that nothing would ever get better. Her parents heard it, and that same day they took her to the school counsellor, who listened and arranged to meet her again the next week.

qa.q: What did Ritu sort into three piles?
qa.a: She sorted her lost marks into gaps in knowledge, poor use of time and careless slips.

qa.q: How does Sachin's thinking after the result differ from Ritu's, and what followed?
qa.a: Sachin decided one failure ruined his future and stopped studying, without checking any evidence. Ritu looked at her answer sheet and found that rushing the last section cost most of her marks.

qa.q: What was Meera feeling when she said nothing would ever get better?
qa.a: She was hopeless and very sad, and needed more than willpower, which is why her parents took her to the counsellor.

qa.q: What could Sachin do now?
qa.a: He could look at his paper with a teacher to see what really happened, and talk to a parent or counsellor about how he feels. 🤍

grounding: Four students face a low result by pausing before deciding, analysing the answer sheet, assuming a ruined future, and seeking a counsellor when hopelessness stays.

passage: Four college students wanted to earn a little on the side. Jahnavi wrote down which skills she had, among them teaching, design and typing, then counted the hours left after classes, so her plan would fit her real week. Kiran worked out what each job would cost him, how long it took and what a fair hourly rate would be. He saw that his first price barely covered data and travel. Ojas watched videos that promised easy money from trading and paid schemes and signed up without checking anything. He risked his savings and time and learned no real skill. Meera spent a month on teaching, freelance jobs and data entry, and compared what each paid per hour. Data entry paid least for the effort, so she dropped it and kept the other two.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi count after writing down her skills?
qa.a: She counted the hours left after classes.

qa.q: How does Ojas's way of choosing differ from Meera's, and what did each gain?
qa.a: Ojas joined schemes he saw in videos without checking, risking savings and learning nothing. Meera compared hourly earnings across three jobs and dropped the one that paid least.

qa.q: What might Ojas be feeling after he has risked his savings?
qa.a: He is probably worried and disappointed, since the promised easy money did not come and he gained no skill.

qa.q: What could Ojas do to start earning safely?
qa.a: He could list skills he already has, ask a trusted adult about any scheme before joining it, and try a small real job such as tutoring. 🙂

grounding: Four students plan side income by listing skills and free hours, tracking costs and pricing, chasing easy-money videos, and dropping the weakest option.

passage: On a sunny afternoon, four toddlers were trying to get onto the sofa. Aparna lay on her tummy across the cushion, then hooked a knee up, then rolled sideways, and stayed with the way that got her knee over the edge. Pallavi had watched her older brother turn round, sit and swing his legs up. She copied the order of it loosely and ended up half on the seat, nearer than she had ever got. Kamal scrambled up the high arm of the sofa rather than the seat. He slipped, and his grandmother, standing beside him, caught him before he hit the floor. Little Divya had once got a knee onto the edge of the cushion, and it had helped. Now she began each climb that way, and she got quicker every day.

qa.q: Who caught Kamal when he slipped?
qa.a: His grandmother caught him.

qa.q: How does Kamal's climb differ from Aparna's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Kamal scrambled at the tall armrest and slipped, needing to be caught, while Aparna tried several ways and stayed with the one that worked.

qa.q: What might Kamal be feeling right after he slips?
qa.a: He is probably startled and maybe a little scared, since he was so eager that he did not check the spot.

qa.q: How could a caregiver help Kamal climb more safely?
qa.a: A caregiver could stay close, guide him to the seat rather than the armrest, and show the knee-first way that worked for others. 🙂

grounding: Four toddlers climb onto a sofa by trial and error, copying an older sibling, scrambling impulsively, and repeating a move that worked.

passage: Four children were planning projects for the science fair. Parveen wrote ten questions she wondered about, including if plants lean towards light. She picked the one she could test with whatever was at home within her deadline. Tenzin planned to grow beans in a pair of cups, one by the window and the other in a dark cupboard. Same soil, same water and same-sized cups, he decided, or the test would not be fair. Rohit chose to construct a volcano that flashed lights and made noise, like his friend's. He ran short of both hours and supplies, and his project stayed half done. Bhavna grew beans too, and one plant in the dark shot up taller than she expected. Then she realised she had left the cupboard open. She did it all over with the cupboard closed, and the result was much clearer.

qa.q: How many cups did Tenzin use for his beans?
qa.a: Tenzin used two cups.

qa.q: How does Rohit's choice of project differ from Parveen's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Rohit chose an elaborate volcano he could not finish and ended with a half-done project. Parveen picked a question she could test with whatever was at home within her deadline.

qa.q: What was Rohit probably feeling when his project stayed half done?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and embarrassed, since he had wanted a project as impressive as his friend's.

qa.q: What could Rohit do for his next project?
qa.a: He could choose a simpler idea he can finish, gather materials early and plan time for each step. 🙂

grounding: Children plan a science fair project by choosing one question, setting a fair test, picking a fancy project they cannot finish, and repeating an odd result.

passage: Before the party, four teens each thought about what they would do if someone pushed them to do something unsafe. Kabir decided in advance what he would not do, such as getting into a car with a careless driver or trying substances; that way his choices in the moment would follow a rule he had already thought through. Sunaina prepared a short line, "No thanks, I'm good," and agreed a code word with her mother for a pick-up, so leaving would need no argument. Rehan feared his friends would find him dull and joined a risky dare. Dread of losing his place felt bigger than the danger just then, and the consequences landed on him alone. Dev, after a risky evening, admitted to himself it was a mistake. He told his parents what had happened, and they listened without shouting and made a plan with him that same night. He chose different company, an earlier time to leave, and one strict rule for next time.

qa.q: What did Sunaina agree with her mother?
qa.a: She agreed on a code word for a pick-up.

qa.q: How does Rehan's reason for joining the dare differ from Kabir's preparation, and what followed?
qa.a: Rehan feared being called boring and joined a risky dare, with consequences falling on him alone. Kabir decided in advance what he would not do, so a rule guided him in the moment.

qa.q: What might Dev be feeling when he tells his parents what happened?
qa.a: He is probably worried and ashamed, but wants to make it right, which is why he tells them instead of hiding it.

qa.q: What could Rehan do now?
qa.a: He could tell a trusted adult what happened, decide firm limits for next time, and prepare a refusal line and exit plan like Sunaina's. 🤍

grounding: Four teens meet pressure to do something unsafe by deciding limits in advance, preparing a refusal and exit, going along to avoid exclusion, and reviewing after giving in.
